prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength to reach a new regime of accuracy and stability in time measurement

statement.case_for: I opened with IceCube (B032) because I weigh most heavily a clue found in nature, but I now think the optical lattice clock is the better prize for this year. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal is a short, original idea. Ye's group then took it to fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 and used it to show many-body effects and millimetre-scale gravitational redshift. The result has been reproduced in many laboratories over two decades. It underpins tests of fundamental constants and dark-sector searches and the coming redefinition of the second. The attribution is clean with two names, which almost no other shortlisted candidate offers. Four colleagues ranked it first and two ranked it second, so it also has the broadest support. I do not treat that support as a measure of merit. I reach the conclusion on the physics and on how cleanly credit can be assigned.
statement.case_against: This is a prize for an instrument and a measurement capability more than for a new phenomenon in nature, and I weigh that heavily. The committee has already honoured the frequency comb (2005) and the control of single trapped ions (2012), so it can fairly be argued that this is a refinement of a line already recognised. The redefinition of the second has not yet happened, and the lattice-clock concept has competitors (ion clocks, other strontium and ytterbium groups) outside the credited names. By contrast B032 delivered a genuinely new window on the universe, and I fear we are choosing the more comfortable attribution over the more consequential discovery. If the source picture for NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane keeps sharpening, B032 may well be the stronger case in a year or two.

responses.point: Pearce ranked B004 first for its clean two-name attribution and maturity, and put IceCube second while noting that his own field is close to it and that credit within a collaboration of hundreds is hard to settle.
responses.response: I agree that attribution is the sharpest difference between the two. I had named Halzen, Karle and Yoshida, but I based that on my own recollection of roles and could not verify it. Your caution about the collaboration persuades me that a three-name IceCube prize would be contested in a way the lattice-clock prize would not. I would not let your proximity to the field exclude B032 from our discussion, because it is a scientific merit question we can all assess. It does mean that you should not be the one to drive that case.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked B004 first, but flagged that the committee must judge how distinct it is from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes and that others share the lattice-clock concept. She also noted that Jun Ye appears in another candidate, so configurations should be coordinated.
responses.response: I take the distinctness question seriously and it is my main reservation. My answer is that the comb made precision optical frequency counting possible and the ion work showed control of single quantum systems. The lattice clock adds something neither did: a large ensemble of neutral atoms interrogated in a lattice free of motional shifts, which gives both stability and accuracy. That is a new regime and not a refinement. On Ye's other candidate, no such candidate is on this shortlist, so there is no conflict in practice. I would still like your view on whether Takamoto and the other Sr-lattice contributors outside the credited names change how we word the citation.

responses.point: Johansson ranked B034 (circuit QED) first and B004 only eighth, citing overlap with earlier prizes in precision spectroscopy and time standards, and noted that the 2025 prize is adjacent to circuit QED.
responses.response: I disagree on B004. Overlap in subject area is not overlap in discovery, and by that logic circuit QED, which sits next to the 2025 superconducting-circuit prize, would be penalised more heavily than the clocks. You acknowledge that tension yourself. I also note you work in that subfield and say you weigh familiarity cautiously, which I respect. My own difficulty with B034 is simpler: four credited names for three places, with Blais or Girvin omitted, and a timing problem so soon after 2025. I do not find that the same objection applies to the clocks.

responses.point: Eriksson ranked dynamical mean-field theory (B027) first as a controlled, non-perturbative framework for correlated electrons with three decades of use, while acknowledging doubt about whether a method counts as a discovery.
responses.response: DMFT is a real intellectual achievement and I do not dismiss it, but I share your own worry. It is a method, and the physical discovery it enabled, such as the Mott transition picture, is harder to point to as a clue found in nature. Only you ranked it in your top eight, so I would want to hear what the other members who work in condensed matter think before it competes with candidates with broader support. I also doubt that DMFT can match a clock for clarity of citation.

responses.point: Mehlig ranked B004 first and B023 (Cirac and Zoller) second, arguing that theory-only recognition after experimental validation is timely.
responses.response: I agree with you on B004. On B023 I am more reserved than you. I ranked it seventh because the decisive link is the experimental realisation by Wineland, Blatt, Monroe and others, and Wineland was already honoured in 2012. A prize for the blueprint alone, after the experiments were partly recognised, sits awkwardly with how I think about discovery. I would not rule out B023 as an alternative, but I do not think it should come ahead of B004.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards a metrology and instrument advance as weighty enough compared with a discovery in nature such as IceCube, and whether the overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes is judged as lowering novelty.
Whether credit for the lattice-clock concept should be widened or the citation phrased to reflect Takamoto and other strontium and ytterbium groups outside the credited names.
Whether the IceCube source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, Galactic plane) will firm up enough, and whether a defensible three-name allocation exists within the collaboration.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My documented connections are to David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theoretical-physics group, and none of them is among the credited names. I work in string theory, gravitation and cosmology, which is not close to any shortlisted field.
